# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: MCP lets AI work with your CMS, not just talk about it

values.value: The Model Context Protocol gives an AI assistant real, typed tools. This blog was modelled, filled with content and published through them, with no clicking through the backoffice.

value.markup:
Chat assistants have been able to describe how to change a website for a long time. What they could not do was change it. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) closes that gap: a server publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a description and a typed schema, and any MCP-aware assistant can discover and call them.

For a CMS like Umbraco that is a big deal. Document types, data types, templates, media and content all become things an assistant can inspect and edit through the same management API the backoffice uses.

values.value: Tools, not guesswork. Photo: Chris Ried on Unsplash.
The assistant stops guessing what your system looks like and starts asking it.
The MCP Blog

value.markup:
Why that is awesome

  • It is grounded. The assistant reads real document types and real data types before it writes anything.
  • It is checkable. Every call is a discrete, logged action, so you can read back exactly what changed.
  • It respects your rules. Conventions such as folders, aliases and block rendering are followed because the assistant works inside the project, not around it.

This very site is the demo: five block types, two block grids and two page types were created over MCP.

input.name: One protocol, every tool: the USB-C moment for AI

values.value: Before MCP every assistant needed a bespoke integration for every tool. One open standard turns that N-by-M problem into plug and play.

value.markup:
Remember when every phone had its own charger? Integrating an AI assistant with your tools used to be the same story: one custom connector per assistant, per tool. Ten assistants and ten tools meant a hundred integrations, all slightly different and all slowly rotting.

MCP replaces that with a single, open contract. A tool is wrapped once as an MCP server, and every MCP client can use it. Build once, plug in anywhere.

values.value: One standard connector for everything. Photo: Hal Gatewood on Unsplash.
Write the integration once. Every assistant that speaks MCP can use it.
The MCP Blog

value.markup:
What you get in practice

  • Portability. Swap assistants without rewriting your tooling.
  • Discoverability. Tools describe themselves, so a client learns what is possible at runtime.
  • Local control. A server can run on your own machine, with your own credentials and a scope you choose, as this project's .mcp.json does.

That is why MCP feels less like a feature and more like infrastructure: it is the boring, standard plug that makes everything else work together.

**View it** at https://localhost:44317/ (HTTP: http://localhost:41576). It's running now from `dotnet run` in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco`. The backoffice login is `admin@example.com` / `1234567890`.

- **Modeling (MCP):**
  - Five block types in the Blocks folder: `heroBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock` and `blogPostListBlock`.
  - Two block grid data types, "Blog Front Page Blocks" and "Blog Post Blocks".
  - Two page types in the Pages folder, `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost`, each with a template.
  - I edited the scaffold's `siteRoot` type so the front page can sit under WWW.
- **Content (MCP):**
  - A published "The MCP Blog" front page under WWW, with the domain `/`. Its grid has a hero block and a "Latest posts" list block.
  - Two published posts about why MCP is awesome. Each has a hero image and a grid of rich text, image and quote blocks.
  - Six Unsplash photos imported into a "Blog" media folder, with photographer credits in the captions.
- **Razor (after the rebuild):**
  - Pages render with `Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`.
  - Each block has an adapter in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml`, a plain model in `Models/Blocks/`, a ViewComponent in `ViewComponents/`, and its markup in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - There are also a shared `_Layout`, a `PostHeader` ViewComponent for the post header, and a few rich-text styles added to `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend/src/site.css`.
  - I ran `npm install` and `npm run build`, which writes `wwwroot/dist/site.css`. All images go through `GetCropUrl`.

**Checks:** both posts, all five image URLs and the CSS return 200. The front page lists both posts, newest first.

**Things to know**
- Nothing is broken that I found. I only inspected the HTML and requests, not the pages in a browser, so the visual styling is untested.
- The `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml` default pointed at `Umbraco.Cms.Web.Common.PublishedModels`, but the generated models are in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models`. I changed the import.
- The post list adapter reads the current page from `UmbracoContext` rather than a friendly extension. That is the one place I wasn't sure of the convention.
- `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` in `.mcp.json` is the scaffold's own setting for the dev certificate. I left it alone.
